content:
When I proposed the integrated explicit analytic number theory network structure last year, I was basing my model on existing collaborative, mostly human-generated formalization projects (PNT, Carleson, etc.) in which we tried to maintain a coherent blueprint with reusable code to assist human formalizers (who might receive some modest assistance from 2025-level AI tools) to fill in various lemma-level sorries, in one large common repository.

However, in August 2026 we are now in an era where entire papers can in principle be autoformalized without regards to any carefully curated common base library, using extremely large, non-human-readable formalizations that take a non-trivial amount of time to typecheck. Already many of the papers partially formalized by the existing IEANTN contain such code, but I do not see this system scaling out to a larger range of papers than we are currently targeting.

I am therefore thinking of radically rethinking the IEANTN structure, inspired by the "Challenge / Solution" paradigm of Lean comparator that is for instance used by the recently launched Palomar registry (that I am also involved in). In this new structure, the core IEANTN would consist of a network of challenge files (and a bunch of supporting Defs.lean type files that mostly contain definitions rather than theorems). As a first approximation, each challenge file would correspond to a given paper, with the challenge file for paper A being a human-readable Lean file asserting that the main results of paper A would follow from the main results of various papers B, C, D cited in the references to that paper, as well as some purely computational results that may be beyond the ability of Lean to currently certify. (Eventually, these computational results may be spun off into their own separate challenge files; and there may be auxiliary challenge files created in due course that are not directly associated to a given paper in the literature but reflect some sort of "folklore knowledge" in the subject that needs to be recorded somewhere, e.g., basic estimates on the zeta function). Then, we would also aim to create (almost certainly using modern AI autoformalizers) large solution files for each challenge file that verify the claims in that solution file; but these files would be checked once using Comparator and basically not touched afterwards (unless the challenge file needs to update for some reason). In particular, these large solution files would not be part of the core IEANTN build.

I am still trying to think my way through what is the correct way to refactor this project (including whether it should be spun off to a separate repository than PNT+, now that there is less code reuse), and would appreciate any thoughts on this.

I think a natural direction would be to make IEANTN more explicitly domain-specific, centered on analytic number theory and on maintaining the dependency graph between papers, auxiliary results, and computational inputs (I usually like to work with a clear taxonomy). In my view, if the large AI-generated solutions are no longer intended to form a reusable common codebase, then separating IEANTN from PNT+ would also make sense.

I would probably first try to define more precisely what the responsibility of IEANTN should be, and what should instead be handled by the other projects that are emerging around the same workflow, such as Palomar, Tau Ceti, Formal Frontier, Formal Conjectures, and Math-Challenge.

I think there is a real risk of ending up with a collection of loosely connected projects that each rebuild parts of the same infrastructure. My idea would be to make these projects interoperate as much as possible and assign fairly clear responsibilities to each of them, so that challenge formats, verification, registries, reusable libraries, and domain-specific dependency graphs are not independently reimplemented several times.

Given what AxiomMath did for bounded gap, and what they claimed to be "reusable" for other formalization projects, I couldn't help but think that they could have done the same (especially the beautiful blueprint) for IEANTN. How were these things decided? Could they have better coordinated this? Of course there's big money involved.

Given the current repo size and build time I think that moving the IEANTN things into different repo(s) would be a good idea. PNT could just keep the core PNT result and variants. Perhaps anything which could possibly be upstreamed to Mathlib should stay in PNT.
